title: Keys — Super, Candidate, Primary, Foreign
summary: The four key types that enforce row identity and cross-table links, and the natural-vs-surrogate decision every schema forces you to make.

slides.markdown:
A **key** is a way of saying "this attribute (or set of attributes) uniquely identifies a row." Every relational schema decision — how you name IDs, how tables reference each other, what a unique-constraint violation means — traces back to this one idea.

There's a hierarchy: **superkey** → **candidate key** → **primary key**, each narrowing the last. Then **foreign keys** use one table's key to point at another. Get keys wrong and you get duplicate customers, orphaned orders, or a schema that can't enforce the rules your business actually needs.

This is the single most interview-tested vocabulary in relational databases — expect it in the first five minutes of almost any DB-adjacent interview.

slides.sectionTitle: Superkey to candidate key to primary key: narrowing down
slides.markdown:
A **superkey** is any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row — including redundant ones. `{employee_id, name}` is a superkey if `employee_id` alone is already unique; adding `name` doesn't break uniqueness, it just adds noise.

A **candidate key** is a *minimal* superkey — remove any attribute and it stops being unique. `{employee_id}` alone is a candidate key; `{employee_id, name}` is not, because it isn't minimal. A table can have multiple candidate keys — `employee_id` and, separately, `email` might each independently identify a row.

The **primary key** is the one candidate key the schema designer picks to be *the* official identifier, used for foreign-key references and typically the clustering key. Every other candidate key still deserves a `UNIQUE` constraint — losing that enforcement is a common oversight.

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing a primary key: natural vs surrogate keys
slides.markdown:
A **natural key** already exists in the real-world data — an email, a national ID, an SKU. A **surrogate key** is manufactured purely for the database — an auto-incrementing integer or a UUID with no business meaning at all.

Natural keys feel appealing because they avoid a "meaningless" extra column, but real-world identifiers change more often than people expect: emails get reassigned, SKUs get renumbered after a reorg, national ID schemes vary by country and sometimes get reissued. When a natural key changes, every foreign key pointing at it has to cascade-update, which is expensive and risky at scale.

Most production schemas default to a surrogate primary key (`id BIGINT` or `UUID`) precisely because it's guaranteed stable, and keep the natural identifier as a separately `UNIQUE`-constrained candidate key for lookups.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: foreign key linking two tables
slides.markdown:
![Foreign key in Orders referencing the primary key in Customers](assets/foreign-key-reference.svg)

A **foreign key** is an attribute (or set of attributes) in one table that must match a candidate key — almost always the primary key — of another table (or be `NULL`, if allowed). It's how relations reference each other without pointers: purely by value.

`Orders.customer_id` referencing `Customers.id` means the database itself refuses to let an order point at a customer that doesn't exist — this is **referential integrity**, enforced by the engine, not by application code discipline.

slides.sectionTitle: Composite keys and when they're unavoidable
slides.markdown:
A **composite key** is a candidate (or primary) key made of more than one attribute, where no single attribute in it is unique alone. A classic case: a `enrollments` table linking students to courses — `(student_id, course_id)` together identify a row, but neither column alone does, since a student has many enrollments and a course has many students.

Composite keys are unavoidable for pure many-to-many junction tables (§ later topic), but they add friction: every foreign key referencing the table now needs both columns, and ORMs historically handled composite keys awkwardly. A common compromise is a surrogate single-column primary key (`enrollment_id`) plus a `UNIQUE (student_id, course_id)` constraint that still enforces "no duplicate enrollment" without forcing every consumer to carry two columns.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: natural vs surrogate key trade-offs
slides.markdown:
| | Natural key | Surrogate key |
|---|---|---|
| Stability | Can change with real-world events (reissued IDs, renamed SKUs) | Never changes — has no business meaning to change |
| Readability | Meaningful in logs/URLs (e.g. `/orders/ORD-2024-881`) | Opaque (`/orders/48213`) unless you expose a separate code |
| Storage/join cost | Often wider (strings), slower joins | Typically a small integer or UUID — fast joins |
| Uniqueness guarantee | Depends on an external authority being correct | Guaranteed by the database itself |

**How to decide:** default to a surrogate primary key for internal joins and foreign keys; keep the natural identifier as a `UNIQUE` column for external lookups and display. Switch to natural-only when the identifier is provably permanent and external systems already depend on it as the join key (e.g. ISO country codes).

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: nullable columns in a candidate key
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll make `email` a candidate key with a `UNIQUE` constraint, but leave it nullable since not every user has verified one yet."

**Why it's wrong:** most engines treat `NULL` as *not equal to anything, including another `NULL`*, so a `UNIQUE` constraint lets in unlimited rows with `email = NULL` — the uniqueness guarantee silently doesn't apply to the case you probably care about most (rows missing the value). This surprises people who assume `UNIQUE` means "no duplicates, period."

**Correct model:** a true candidate key must be both unique *and* non-null (this is literally the entity-integrity rule for primary keys, and good practice for any candidate key). If a value is genuinely optional, either don't make it a candidate key, or add a partial/filtered unique index (`WHERE email IS NOT NULL`) so the constraint means what you intended.

slides.sectionTitle: What a foreign key actually enforces at write time
slides.markdown:
A foreign key isn't just documentation — it's a runtime check the engine executes on every `INSERT`/`UPDATE` to the referencing table and every `DELETE`/`UPDATE` to the referenced table. Insert an order with `customer_id = 999` when no customer 999 exists, and the engine rejects it with a constraint-violation error before the row is written.

That check has a real cost: it's effectively an index lookup on the referenced table for every write, which is why the referenced column (`customers.id`) needs its own index — it already has one for free since it's the primary key, but a foreign key on a *non-indexed* column can silently make every insert into the child table do a full scan of the parent table to validate.

This is a real production gotcha: adding a foreign key to a large table without an index on the referenced column can turn a fast bulk import into a multi-hour job.

slides.sectionTitle: UUID vs auto-increment integer as a surrogate key
slides.markdown:
| | Auto-increment integer | UUID |
|---|---|---|
| Size | 4-8 bytes | 16 bytes |
| Generation | Requires a round-trip to the database (or a sequence) | Can be generated client-side, before an insert |
| Predictability | Sequential — leaks row count/creation order, guessable | Random (v4) — doesn't leak information |
| Index locality | New rows append to the end of the index — cheap | Random UUIDs scatter inserts across the whole index, hurting cache locality |
| Merging across systems | Collides if two systems both start at 1 | Collision-free across distributed systems by design |

**How to decide:** pick auto-increment for a single-writer system where index locality matters and leaking row order is fine; pick UUID (ideally UUIDv7 or similar time-ordered variant) when IDs must be generated offline/client-side or merged across multiple writers, and accept the index-locality cost or mitigate it with a time-ordered UUID variant.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: the cost of an unindexed foreign key at scale
slides.markdown:
Concretely: bulk-loading 1 million child rows against a parent table of 1 million rows, if the referenced column has no index, means up to 1 million full scans of the parent — an O(n²) operation that can turn a job expected to take seconds into one that takes hours or never finishes within a maintenance window.

With the referenced column properly indexed (which it is automatically if it's a primary key), each check is an O(log n) B-tree lookup — the same load finishes in low seconds. This is why "why is this migration stuck" incidents so often trace back to a foreign key added against a column someone forgot to index, usually a rarely-used lookup table's non-PK column.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reusing a deleted primary key value
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We deleted customer 42, so it's fine to let the sequence eventually reassign 42 to a new customer — the old one is gone anyway."

**Why it's wrong:** primary keys often leak into logs, external systems, support tickets, cached data, and soft-deleted or archived records that still reference the old ID. Reassigning 42 to a genuinely different customer means any of those stale references now silently point at the wrong entity — a support agent pulling up "customer 42" from an old ticket could see someone else's data.

**Correct model:** treat surrogate keys as **never reused**, even after deletion — standard auto-increment sequences already guarantee this (they only move forward), and it should stay true for any custom ID scheme too. If you need to reclaim identifiers for a compliance reason, that's a deliberate, audited process, not a side effect of normal auto-increment behavior.
